title: Public Goods & the State
hook: Some things markets struggle to provide — clean air, national defense, street lighting — because no one can be charged for them. That gap is a core reason states exist.
key_points: A public good is non-excludable (hard to charge for) and non-rival (one person's use doesn't reduce another's).
Markets tend to under-provide them because of the 'free-rider' problem.
Examples: national defense, clean air, public health, basic research, street lighting.
This 'market failure' is a classic economic justification for government provision.
content_html: Markets are good at providing many things, but they systematically struggle with a particular category economists call public goods. A public good has two defining features. It is non-excludable: once it exists, it is hard or impossible to stop people who didn't pay from enjoying it — you cannot easily withhold national defense or clean air from a single non-payer. And it is non-rival: one person benefiting doesn't use it up for others — your enjoyment of street lighting doesn't dim it for your neighbor.
extra_html: These features create the "free-rider problem." If people can benefit whether or not they pay, each individual has an incentive to let others foot the bill — and if everyone reasons that way, the good is under-produced or never produced at all, even though society would gladly pay for it collectively. A private company cannot easily profit from something it can't charge people to use. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes this is a classic case of "market failure": a situation where free markets, left alone, don't deliver an efficient or adequate outcome. It is one of the oldest and least ideologically loaded justifications for government: the state can fund public goods through taxation that everyone contributes to, solving the collective-action problem markets cannot. Defense, public health, basic scientific research, clean air, and the legal system itself are often cited examples — which is part of why even thinkers skeptical of large government usually accept a core role for the state here.

related.title: What Public Policy Is
related.hook: Passing a law is just the start. Public policy is the whole arc — from defining a problem to actually delivering a solution and seeing whether it worked.

related.title: Taxation & Public Budgets
related.hook: A government's budget is its values written in numbers — and taxation is how it raises the money to act at all. Follow the money to understand the priorities.

related.title: What Government Is For
related.hook: Every society needs a way to make and enforce collective decisions — that shared system of authority is what we call government.

related.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
related.hook: When everyone shares a resource but no one owns it, each person's rational choice can add up to collective ruin. That trap explains a huge slice of environmental politics.

flashcards.prompt: What two features define a 'public good' in economics?
flashcards.back_html: It is non-excludable (hard to stop non-payers using it) and non-rival (one person's use doesn't diminish another's).

choices.text: People can enjoy a good without paying, so markets under-provide it
Public transport that is always free to use
A rule that bans charging for any service

flashcards.explanation_html: If no one can be excluded, individuals have little incentive to pay, so private provision falls short of what society needs.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the existence of public goods used to justify government action?

choices.text: It is a 'market failure' — the state can provide what markets under-supply
Because markets always provide too much of everything
Because public goods are illegal to sell

flashcards.explanation_html: When markets predictably under-provide essential goods, collective provision funded by taxation is a standard economic rationale for the state.
